svg.aria-label: Map of downtown Vancouver comparing the 1967 freeway plan with the city as built

g.data-note: Elevated freeway along Burrard Inlet in the 1967 Vancouver Transportation Study, running through the Project 200 waterfront scheme. Line is approximate. Source: History essay
g.title: Waterfront freeway · approx.

g.data-note: The route swung through Gastown's Maple Tree Square and the heart of Chinatown at Carrall Street. Source: History essay; connectors along Carrall and Gore: Wikipedia: Strathcona, Vancouver
g.title: Maple Tree Sq & Carrall St · approx.
g.text: Maple Tree Sq & Carrall St · approx.

g.data-note: A connector along Gore Avenue that would have partly destroyed Chinatown and Gastown. Source: Wikipedia: Strathcona, Vancouver
g.title: Gore Ave connector · approx.

g.data-note: East along the Prior Street corridor toward Highway 1, through the south of Strathcona. Sources: History essay; Wikipedia: Strathcona, Vancouver
g.title: Prior St corridor to Hwy 1 · approx.
g.text: Prior St corridor to Hwy 1 · approx.

g.data-note: More routes would have run south along the Columbia and Quebec corridors. Exact alignment unknown; drawn on today’s streets. Source: History essay
g.title: Columbia / Quebec corridors · approx.

g.data-note: By 1969 the favoured design was a tunnel reached by a causeway near Brockton Point. Council funded the approaches 6–5 in Dec 1971; dead by end of 1972. North Shore landing not sourced. Source: History essay
g.title: Third crossing: causeway + tunnel · approx.

g.data-note: The new Georgia Viaduct would carry freeway traffic straight into downtown. It was built; the rest was not. Sources: History essay; geometry OpenStreetMap
g.title: Georgia viaduct link (built 1971–72)

g.data-note: The freeway would have cut through its heart at Carrall St. Council moved to approve that first segment on June 1, 1967; hearings forced by merchants and residents stopped it. Source: History essay
g.title: CHINATOWN

g.data-note: Targeted for “urban renewal”: some 15 blocks were bulldozed, including most of Hogan’s Alley, and a freeway was proposed through its south. Sources: History essay; Wikipedia: Strathcona, Vancouver
g.title: STRATHCONA

g.data-note: Park Lane and nearby blocks, between Union and Prior from about Main to Jackson; the heart of Vancouver’s Black community. Its western half was levelled from 1967 for the viaducts. Sources: History essay; Wikipedia: Hogan's Alley, Vancouver
g.title: HOGAN'S ALLEY · approx.

g.data-note: Maple Tree Square sat in the path of the waterfront route. Source: History essay
g.title: GASTOWN

g.data-note: CPR/Marathon Realty plan for towers, plazas and parking over the tracks with the freeway through it. Granville Square (1973) is the main piece built. Source: History essay
g.title: WATERFRONT · PROJECT 200

g.data-note: The crossing’s causeway would have landed near Brockton Point, at the edge of Stanley Park. Source: History essay
g.title: STANLEY PARK APPROACH

g.data-note: Opened 1971 and 1972: the only part of the freeway system built. Council voted to remove them in 2015; the 2018 Northeast False Creek Plan replaces them with streets, parks and housing. Still standing; timeline “still uncertain.” Source: History essay; geometry OpenStreetMap
g.title: Georgia & Dunsmuir viaducts

g.data-note: Chinatown survived; the 1967 route through it was dropped. Boundary: OpenStreetMap. Source: History essay
g.title: Chinatown · still here

g.data-note: Residents (SPOTA, founded 1968) won repair instead of clearance; Vincent Massey Award, 1975. Boundary: OpenStreetMap. Source: History essay
g.title: Strathcona · rehabilitated

g.data-note: Maple Tree Square and Gastown were spared. Source: History essay; Wikipedia: Hogan's Alley, Vancouver
g.title: Gastown · still here

g.data-note: The City has a memorandum of understanding with the Hogan’s Alley Society for the 898 Main Street block. Position approximate. Source: History essay
g.title: 898 Main · Hogan’s Alley Society

g.data-note: SkyTrain, opened December 1985. Geometry: OpenStreetMap. Source: History essay
g.title: Expo Line

g.data-note: SkyTrain to Richmond and YVR. Geometry: OpenStreetMap. Source: History essay
g.title: Canada Line

g.data-note: Has crossed Burrard Inlet since 1977. Route: OpenStreetMap. Source: Future essay
g.title: SeaBus

g.data-note: Begun around Stanley Park in 1917; the City counts 28 km of uninterrupted waterfront path. OSM-tagged seawall segments shown. Source: History essay
g.title: Seawall · 28 km in all

g.data-note: Homes on former railway and industrial land along Burrard Inlet. Source: History essay
g.title: Coal Harbour

g.data-note: Expo 86 site sold in 1988; filled in with housing and parks over two decades. Source: History essay
g.title: False Creek North

g.data-note: Planned by the City in 1974, built from 1975: co-ops and mixed-income housing. Source: History essay
g.title: False Creek South

g.data-note: Stanley Park Causeway and Lions Gate Bridge, the existing route through the park. No third crossing was built. Geometry: OpenStreetMap. Source: History essay
g.title: Lions Gate approach today
